title: Single-Molecule Fluorescence Imaging in Living Saccharomyces cerevisiae Cells
protocol: Streak yeast cells onto a YPD plate four days before imaging.
In the morning on the day before imaging, inoculate one colony of yeast into 1 mL of SC medium.
Grow the culture at 30°C while shaking/rotating.
In the evening, dilute cultures into prewarmed medium (30°C) to achieve an optical density (OD600) of ~0.2–0.4 in the morning.
If growth rate is unknown, make a dilution series for strains exhibiting wildtype growth rates.
For glucose, add 1 μL of culture in 5 mL of fresh medium.
For raffinose or galactose, add 2 μL of culture in 2 mL of fresh medium.
Measure the OD600 of the yeast cultures using a spectrophotometer.
If the OD600 is below 0.2, grow cells for a few more hours.
If the OD600 is between 0.2 and 0.8, proceed to steps below.
If the OD600 is above 0.8, dilute culture to OD600 0.1–0.2 in prewarmed SC medium and grow them for two cell-cycles (around 180 min for strains with wildtype growth rates in glucose).
Spin 1 ml of yeast imaging culture at 3,824 × g for 1 min.
Remove supernatant.
Resuspend cells in 4 μl of prewarmed SC medium with appropriate carbon source by vortexing briefly.
Rinse a cleaned coverslip with 70% ethanol and dry it over a flame without flaming the coverslip directly.
Place the dried coverslip in an Attofluor™ Cell Chamber.
Pipette the entire volume (usually 4–10 μl) onto the coverslip.
Cut a circle out of the agar imaging pad using a 14 mL growth tube.
Place the agar slab on top of the yeast cells.
Press down gently with your thumb to secure the agar slab.
Optionally, place an additional coverslip on top of the agar slab to prevent drying during the experiment.
Wash away any dye used for labeling by resuspending the cells in 1 mL prewarmed medium.
Spin the cells at 3,824 × g for 1 minute and remove the supernatant.
Measure the OD600 of the yeast cultures using a spectrophotometer.
If the OD600 is below 0.2, grow the cells for a few more hours.
If the OD600 is between 0.2 and 0.8, proceed to the next steps.
If the OD600 is above 0.8, dilute the culture to an OD of 0.1–0.2 in prewarmed SC medium.
Grow the diluted cultures for two cell-cycles (around 180 minutes for strains with wildtype growth rates in glucose).
Pipette 300 μL of yeast culture onto a concanavalin A-coated coverslip placed in an Attofluor™ Cell Chamber or glass-bottom dish.
Incubate for 20 minutes at 30°C.
Remove excess medium.
Wash cells by adding 300 μL of prewarmed medium and removing the fluid.
Repeat wash step.
Add 3 mL of prewarmed medium onto the cells.
They are now ready for imaging.
Optional: If labeling with a dye (such as HALO dyes), add an additional wash step after step 1: resuspend the cells in 1 mL prewarmed medium, spin at 3,824 × g for 1 minute and remove supernatant.
Resuspend cells in 300 μL of medium.
Continue with steps 2–7 of the protocol.
Turn on the microscope, camera, and fluorescence light source (lasers or LED).
Turn on the stage incubator and set at correct temperature.
Let the temperature of the incubator stabilize.
Turn on the stage controller.
Open the microscopy software.
Focus on the cells using transmitted light.
Switch to fluorescence excitation.
Move the stage to find a field of view with cells suitable for imaging.
Aim for 50-100 cells in an area of 100 × 100 μm.
Avoid cells that have high levels of autofluorescence.
Set the excitation power to maximum for tracking individual RNAs.
Use 0.1%–1% of the maximum power for imaging gene transcription over time.
Set exposure time to 30-50 ms for tracking individual RNAs.
Use 150 ms exposure time for imaging gene transcription.
For fast processes such as tracking of individual RNAs, perform continuous imaging with no dead time between frames.
For slower processes such as imaging of gene transcription over time, use an interval of 10–30 s between frames.
If available on the microscope, use the autofocus setting to prevent z-drift during acquisition.
Turn on the fluorescence excitation and focus on the center of the cells.
Start acquisition.
Choose optimal excitation power and exposure time to balance signal-to-noise ratio and minimize photobleaching/phototoxicity.
Increase excitation power or exposure time to increase number of emitted photons per acquisition.
Be aware of signs of phototoxicity: sudden uneven fluorescence, termination of fluorescence signal, transcription, and cell division.
Use longer exposure times (150–200 ms) for relatively static spots such as transcription sites or single genomic loci.
For mobile spots like diffusing RNAs, use shorter exposure times (10–50 ms) to avoid blurring due to motion.
Visualize single proteins using laser excitation and inclined illumination (HILO) with an TIRF angle around 60°–65° and laser powers of 10 μW to 10 mW.
Observe diffusing proteins at exposure times of 10–30 ms.
Visualize DNA-bound proteins at exposure times of 500–1,000 ms for dwell time measurements.
Avoid exposure times above 1,000 ms due to cell movement causing blurring.
Place the sample on the microscope stage without covering the imaging dish if adding drugs or compounds during imaging.
Gently open the microscope chamber and slowly add the compound using a micropipette.
Add roughly equal volume of drug as the volume already in the dish for good mixing.
Adjust the focus of the microscope after drug addition.
Alternatively, use an injection lid for drug addition via some stage-top incubator systems.
Make a maximum intensity projection using Fiji.
Segment cells and nuclei using CellProfiler.
